prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's president has defended his government's recent ceasefire in the country's volatile Swat Valley in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece, saying that many in the West have mischaracterized the deal. President Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the troubled region. The permanent ceasefire, which was brokered in late February between members of the Taliban and leaders of Swat Valley, has been criticized and called a major concession by the Pakistani government in an attempt to hold off Taliban attacks. The central government has long exerted little control in the area, but it launched an intense military offensive in late July to flush out militants from areas of the North West Frontier Province . As retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly attacks, beheadings and destruction of girls' schools. They also continued to gain ground, setting up checkpoints throughout the area. President Asif Ali Zardari addressed the international criticism in his Wall Street Journal article, published Wednesday. "We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists," Zardari wrote. "The clerics with whom we have engaged are not Taliban. Indeed, in our dialogue we'd made it clear that it is their responsibility to rein in and neutralize Taliban and other insurgents." The deal was brokered by Sufi Mohammed, a pro-Taliban cleric who in the past was arrested for leading thousands of fighters against the United States in Afghanistan. Mohammed made the deal with his son-in-law and Taliban commander Maulana Fazlullah. In the article, Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the region. "We have not and will not condone the closing of girls' schools, as we saw last year when militants closed schools in pockets of Swat Valley. Indeed, the government insists that the education of young women is mandatory. This is not an example of the government condoning or capitulating to extremism -- quite the opposite," Zardari wrote. The cease-fire deal imposes Islamic law, or sharia, in the region. As part of the agreement, the Taliban is allowing boys' schools to reopen and the government to set up temporary quarters for the more than 200,000 Swat residents who fled. Women in the area interviewed by CNN said that they would not be able to go to the schools and that, under Taliban-imposed sharia law, they cannot even be seen in public without their husbands or fathers. Swat Valley, located in North West Frontier Province, was once one of Pakistan's biggest tourist destinations. It is near the Afghanistan border and is 300 kilometers (186 miles) from the capital, Islamabad. -- CNN's Stan Grant contributed to this report.

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) —** In an opinion article published Wednesday in *The Wall Street Journal*, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari rejected Western criticism of his government’s recent truce in the conflict-ridden Swat Valley, arguing that the agreement has been widely misunderstood. He also insisted that the ceasefire would not result in the closure of schools for girls.

The indefinite truce was negotiated in late February between Taliban members and Swat Valley leaders. Critics have described it as a significant concession by Pakistan’s government intended to prevent further Taliban assaults.

Pakistan’s central authorities have historically maintained limited control over the region. In late July, however, the military began a major operation aimed at driving militants out of parts of the North West Frontier Province. The Taliban responded to the deployment with deadly attacks, beheadings and the destruction of girls’ schools. Militants also expanded their influence and established checkpoints across the area.

Addressing international objections to the agreement, Zardari wrote: “We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists.”

He said the religious leaders involved in the discussions were not members of the Taliban. According to Zardari, the government had made clear during the talks that those clerics were responsible for restraining and neutralizing Taliban fighters and other insurgents.

The agreement was mediated by Sufi Mohammed, a pro-Taliban cleric who was previously arrested after leading thousands of combatants against the United States in Afghanistan. Mohammed negotiated the arrangement with Maulana Fazlullah, his son-in-law and a Taliban commander.

Zardari further maintained that the truce would not permit girls’ schools in Swat to be shut down. He said the government had neither accepted nor intended to accept such closures, including those carried out by militants in parts of the valley the previous year. He added that the government considers education compulsory for young women and argued that the agreement represents resistance to extremism rather than surrender to it.

Under the ceasefire, Islamic law, or sharia, is to be introduced in the region. The Taliban, as part of the arrangement, has agreed to let boys’ schools resume operations and to allow the government to establish temporary accommodation for more than 200,000 people who escaped from Swat.

Women from the region told CNN that they would be unable to attend the schools. They also said Taliban-enforced sharia rules prevent them from appearing in public unless accompanied by their husbands or fathers.

Swat Valley lies in the North West Frontier Province, close to the Afghan border and approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) from Islamabad. It was formerly among Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations.

CNN’s Stan Grant contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about President Asif Ali Zardari defending Pakistan’s ceasefire agreement with militants in the Swat Valley and addressing concerns about girls’ schools and sharia law.
counterfactuals.output:
**Zardari defends Swat peace deal, vows to protect girls’ education**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari has defended a ceasefire agreement with militants in the country’s Swat Valley, rejecting criticism that the government surrendered to extremists by allowing Islamic law to be introduced in the region.

The agreement, negotiated by authorities in Pakistan’s North West Frontier Province, was intended to halt months of fighting between security forces and Taliban militants. In return for a ceasefire, the government agreed to establish a sharia-based judicial system in Swat and surrounding districts.

Zardari said the arrangement was designed to restore peace and provide faster justice, not to hand control of the region to militants. He emphasized that any new courts would operate within Pakistan’s constitution and that the state would retain authority over the area.

The president also addressed concerns about the future of girls’ education. Militants had destroyed or shut down scores of schools in Swat, many of them serving girls, as part of a campaign against education they considered un-Islamic.

Zardari said girls must be allowed to attend school and insisted the government would not accept restrictions that violated constitutional rights. He argued that neither Islam nor the peace agreement prohibited female education.

Critics, including Pakistani human rights activists and Western officials, warned that the deal could embolden militants and create a sanctuary for extremists. Supporters said residents of Swat were exhausted by violence and needed an immediate end to the fighting.

The ceasefire remained fragile, with its success dependent on militants laying down their arms, ending attacks on schools and government institutions, and accepting the authority of the Pakistani state.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy surrounding Pakistan’s Swat Valley ceasefire, including Zardari’s Wall Street Journal op-ed, the Taliban’s role, and the agreement’s impact on women’s education.
counterfactuals.output:
Pakistan’s 2009 Swat Valley ceasefire was controversial because it appeared to trade state authority and civil rights for a fragile pause in Taliban violence.

- **The agreement:** The North-West Frontier Province government negotiated with Sufi Muhammad’s TNSM movement to introduce the *Nizam-e-Adl* regulation—Sharia-based courts in Swat and the wider Malakand region. In return, militants associated with Sufi Muhammad’s son-in-law, Maulana Fazlullah, were expected to stop fighting and disarm. President Asif Ali Zardari later signed the regulation after parliamentary approval.

- **Zardari’s Wall Street Journal argument:** Zardari defended the policy as a conditional peace initiative with local representatives, not a surrender or direct negotiation with terrorists. He stressed that Pakistan remained committed to fighting extremism and suggested that quicker Islamic courts addressed genuine local complaints about a slow and corrupt justice system. Critics considered this distinction artificial because the ceasefire could not function without Fazlullah’s Taliban, who controlled much of Swat by force.

- **The Taliban’s role:** The Taliban used intimidation, executions, floggings and attacks on schools to establish authority before and during the negotiations. They did not reliably disarm and soon pushed beyond Swat into neighboring Buner. Sufi Muhammad also rejected Pakistan’s democratic and judicial system as un-Islamic. These developments reinforced claims that the agreement had legitimized militants and given them time and territory to regroup.

- **Women’s education:** The agreement itself did not formally abolish girls’ education, and the reduction in fighting initially raised hopes that schools could reopen. In practice, however, Taliban edicts had already closed or destroyed many girls’ schools, frightened teachers and families, and imposed strict rules on women’s movement, dress and schooling. Some girls were allowed to return only under restrictive conditions, while older students remained especially vulnerable. Thus, critics argued that the ceasefire effectively left women’s educational rights subject to militant approval.

The arrangement soon unraveled. Taliban expansion and continued abuses prompted a major Pakistani military offensive in spring 2009, underscoring the central criticism that the ceasefire had produced neither durable peace nor meaningful protection for women and other civilians.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
**Zardari Says Swat Ceasefire Is No Concession to Extremists**

**ISLAMABAD —** President Asif Ali Zardari has defended Pakistan’s ceasefire initiative in the northwestern Swat Valley, saying the agreement is intended to restore peace and improve access to justice rather than reward Taliban militants who have waged a violent campaign against the state.

The truce, announced after negotiations between the provincial government and cleric Sufi Muhammad, calls for an end to fighting in Swat and neighboring districts of the Malakand region. In return, the government has agreed in principle to introduce a system of Islamic justice aimed at resolving cases more quickly.

Zardari said the arrangement should not be interpreted as a concession to extremists. The demand for a faster, Sharia-based judicial system in Malakand predates the Taliban insurgency, he argued, and has long been supported by sections of the local population frustrated by slow and expensive courts.

Under the government’s interpretation, the judicial reforms would operate within Pakistan’s Constitution and would not permit militants to impose their own authority. Officials say the agreement is conditional on peace being restored and on armed groups ending attacks on security forces, schools and civilians.

The president’s position reflects Islamabad’s effort to distinguish between responding to local grievances and accepting the political program of Taliban commanders. Pakistani officials maintain that addressing complaints about governance and justice could deprive militants of public support while allowing displaced families to return home and normal life to resume.

The Swat Valley, once one of Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations, has been devastated by an insurgency led by fighters loyal to Maulana Fazlullah. Militants have attacked police stations, executed opponents, destroyed or closed hundreds of schools—many of them for girls—and challenged the authority of the government. Military operations have failed to establish lasting security, while the fighting has displaced large numbers of residents.

The ceasefire was negotiated through Sufi Muhammad, the head of the Tehrik-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Mohammadi and Fazlullah’s father-in-law. After his release from prison, Sufi Muhammad offered to use his influence to persuade militants to halt their campaign. The provincial government in the North-West Frontier Province, now called Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, then announced plans for a new judicial regulation in Malakand.

Zardari and other government leaders contend that the initiative is a peace process, not a surrender. They say the state has not recognized any parallel militant administration, granted immunity for terrorism or abandoned its responsibility to protect citizens. Security forces, officials add, retain the right to respond if militants violate the ceasefire or use the pause to regroup.

The president has also sought to reassure Pakistan’s international partners, particularly the United States and Afghanistan, which fear that peace agreements can give insurgents time and space to consolidate control. Western governments have repeatedly warned that earlier truces in Pakistan’s tribal belt allowed Taliban and Al Qaeda-linked fighters to strengthen their networks and increase attacks across the Afghan border.

Pakistani authorities argue that Swat differs from the tribal areas because the proposed reforms address a specific local demand for an efficient justice system. They also say any lasting settlement requires militants to disarm and accept the authority of the state.

Critics inside Pakistan remain skeptical. Human-rights activists, opposition figures and residents who fled Swat have questioned whether the government can protect women, political workers and religious minorities if militants remain armed. They also fear that introducing religious courts under pressure from insurgents could encourage similar campaigns elsewhere.

Particular concern surrounds girls’ education. Fazlullah’s followers have threatened female students and teachers and destroyed school buildings. Government officials insist that the agreement does not authorize restrictions on education or permit militants to dictate social policy, but activists say enforcement will be the true test.

Zardari’s defense of the ceasefire rests on three central claims: that the judicial changes answer a legitimate local grievance; that the agreement remains subject to Pakistan’s Constitution and parliamentary institutions; and that peace depends on militants ending violence and accepting the state’s authority.

The success of the initiative will therefore be measured not by the announcement of a truce but by developments on the ground—whether attacks cease, schools reopen, displaced residents return and government institutions regain control.

If militants continue to patrol, intimidate residents or administer their own punishments, critics are likely to view the arrangement as capitulation. If violence declines and constitutional authority is restored, Zardari will be able to argue that the government separated a popular demand for justice from the extremists who had exploited it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
Pakistan’s 2009 peace agreement in the Swat Valley drew international criticism because it allowed Islamic law to be introduced in Malakand in return for a Taliban ceasefire. Critics feared the accord would legitimize militants, weaken the state’s authority and give insurgents a protected base near Afghanistan.

U.S. and NATO officials expressed concern that earlier truces in Pakistan had enabled militants to regroup. Afghanistan also warned that concessions in Swat could strengthen cross-border extremists, while human-rights groups highlighted Taliban attacks on women, political opponents and hundreds of girls’ schools.

President Asif Ali Zardari defended the government’s position, insisting that it was dealing with local representatives rather than capitulating to militants. “We are not negotiating with terrorists,” he said, describing the arrangement as an effort to restore peace and justice. He also rejected fears that Taliban restrictions on female education would be accepted: “We will not permit the closure of girls’ schools.”

The government said implementation of the agreement was conditional on the restoration of peace. International skeptics nevertheless argued that enforcement mechanisms were weak and that the militants’ interpretation of Islamic law could undermine constitutional rights, particularly those of women and girls.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a factual CNN-style story covering the February ceasefire in Swat Valley, Sufi Mohammed and Maulana Fazlullah’s involvement, the imposition of sharia, displaced residents, and local women’s concerns.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ceasefire brings uneasy calm to Pakistan’s Swat Valley**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** A ceasefire between Pakistani security forces and Taliban militants brought a tentative calm to the Swat Valley in February 2009, after months of fighting forced hundreds of thousands of residents from their homes and disrupted schools, businesses and public services.

The truce followed an agreement between authorities in Pakistan’s North West Frontier Province, now called Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Sufi Mohammed, the founder of the outlawed Tehrik-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Mohammadi movement.

Under the deal announced February 16, the provincial government agreed to establish a sharia-based judicial system in Swat and the wider Malakand region. In return, Sufi Mohammed was expected to help persuade militants led by his son-in-law, Maulana Fazlullah, to stop fighting.

Fazlullah’s faction had taken control of large parts of Swat, once one of Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations. His militants attacked security forces, executed opponents, destroyed schools and used illegal FM radio broadcasts to promote their strict interpretation of Islam.

After an initial temporary truce, Fazlullah’s representatives announced an indefinite ceasefire. Sufi Mohammed traveled to Swat with supporters and held talks aimed at consolidating the agreement.

Pakistani officials said the new judicial system was intended to provide speedier justice in a region where residents had long complained about slow courts. Critics, however, warned that the deal could legitimize Taliban authority and allow militants time to regroup. The regulation implementing the system still required federal approval and was formally signed by President Asif Ali Zardari in April.

For displaced families, the ceasefire offered hope of returning home, but many remained cautious. Fighting had damaged communities and left residents uncertain about whether the militants or the government would ultimately maintain control.

Women faced particular concerns. Fazlullah’s movement had opposed girls’ education, and militants had destroyed or damaged numerous schools. Women also feared tighter restrictions on employment, movement and access to health care under the militants’ interpretation of sharia.

The ceasefire reduced violence temporarily, but it did not resolve the struggle for Swat. Within months, the agreement unraveled as militants expanded into neighboring districts, prompting a major Pakistani military offensive and another large wave of displacement.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
